extracted.intended_audience: European patent attorneys, patent practitioners and examiners applying the EPO problem-and-solution approach
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluating inventive step under the European Patent Convention using the EPO 'problem and solution approach', including selection of closest prior art, formulation of the objective technical problem, and assessment of obviousness in light of case law and the Guidelines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Problem and solution approach — three main stages
rubrics_metrics.description: In order to assess inventive step in an objective and predictable manner, apply the problem and solution approach which comprises three main stages: (1) determining the 'closest prior art', (2) establishing the 'objective technical problem' to be solved, and (3) considering whether the claimed invention, starting from the closest prior art and the objective technical problem, would have been obvious to the skilled person.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deviation from this approach should be exceptional. The approach constructs a logical chain of arguments (a 'convincing chain of considerations') to demonstrate obviousness or inventive step (Art. 56 EPC).

rubrics_metrics.name: Closest prior art — main selection criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: A document qualifies as closest prior art if it: (a) should have the same or similar purpose or effect as the invention; or (b) should deal with a similar technical problem as the invention or at least belong to the same or a closely related technical field as the claimed invention; or (c) should have a similar use and require minimal structural modifications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The number of features a claim has in common with prior art is not by itself a suitable criterion for selection. Consider purpose/type/use and minimal adaptations rather than simple feature-counting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate/feasible starting point (document suitability)
rubrics_metrics.description: Only documents that are an appropriate/feasible starting point for the assessment of inventive step should be used — i.e. those from which the skilled person had a reasonable chance to arrive at the subject-matter of the claim in an obvious manner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Think in terms of a pre-selection (set) of documents rather than a single 'one and only' closest prior art. If one cannot arrive at the invention from these realistic starting points, one cannot reasonably argue it could be arrived at from other (inappropriate) starting points.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiple equally valid starting points
rubrics_metrics.description: There can be several equally valid starting points for the assessment of inventive step, for example when the skilled person has a choice of several workable solutions which might lead to the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If multiple workable solutions exist, it may be necessary to apply the problem-and-solution approach to each such starting point in turn to establish inventive step; however, to show lack of inventive step it is sufficient to show obviousness starting from one appropriate starting point.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden of proof: showing lack vs presence of inventive step
rubrics_metrics.description: To show that claimed subject-matter does not involve an inventive step, it is sufficient to demonstrate, starting from one appropriate starting point, that it was obvious for the skilled person to arrive at the claimed subject-matter. To show that a claim involves an inventive step, it may be necessary to apply the approach to each plausible starting point.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The assessment strategy differs depending on whether the challenger seeks to demonstrate obviousness (one starting point suffices) or the applicant seeks to establish inventiveness (may require considering all plausible starting points).

rubrics_metrics.name: Closest prior art need not disclose the objective technical problem
rubrics_metrics.description: The closest prior art does not have to disclose the objective technical problem; the objective technical problem is determined in the second step based on the technical effect(s) provided by the features distinguishing the invention from the closest prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A document can be a suitable starting point even if it does not mention or disclose the particular problem later formulated as the objective technical problem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid selecting closest prior art based on feature-counting
rubrics_metrics.description: Selection of the closest prior art should not be based merely on the number of features common to the claim and a prior document.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case law and Guidelines emphasize purpose/type/use and minimal structural changes over raw counts of common features. Relying on feature-counting is an anti-pattern (see T 870/96 example).

rubrics_metrics.name: Obvious/defective or speculative disclosures are unsuitable
rubrics_metrics.description: A prior-art document that is obviously defective (its disclosure cannot be reproduced) or merely speculative about future feasibility is not an appropriate starting point for inventive-step assessment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: T 211/01 (obviously defective disclosure unsuitable), T 1764/09 (speculative review not suitable). The skilled person would not normally consider such disclosures as realistic starting points.

rubrics_metrics.name: Type/genus and purpose indicators (importance of claim preamble)
rubrics_metrics.description: Features that define the type/genus of the subject-matter (often those in the first words of a claim) and indications of purpose are important indicators for selecting an appropriate starting point; an appropriate starting point should be designed for the same purpose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The 'main subject-matter' indicated in the claim (e.g., 'A lawn mower, comprising...') typically points to documents of the same type/genus. Purpose can be implicit in features; small clarifications can change what qualifies as closest prior art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conscious choice defines development framework — switching types unlikely
rubrics_metrics.description: A conscious selection of a starting point generally defines the framework for further development; it is unlikely and normally not obvious for the skilled person to change from the chosen type to a completely different type in the course of development.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case law (e.g. T 1228/08, T 535/10) shows that choosing a starting point in one technical context typically keeps further development within that context; attempting to re-purpose a starting-point item into a different use is usually not an obvious route.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constituent material can disqualify a starting point
rubrics_metrics.description: The main constituent material of a claimed subject-matter can be an indicator for closest prior art; a prior art item made of a different main material may be an unrealistic starting point.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: a 'tool made from metal' would not realistically start from a 'tool made from wood' if the material is central to the invention's development (see T 1228/08 discussion).

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicant's subjective stated purpose cannot dictate closest prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: The purpose of the invention when establishing the closest prior art is determined 'in the light of the application as a whole' and not by subjective statements of purpose in the description that are not achieved by the claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicants cannot influence selection of closest prior art by adding purposes to the description that are not actually realised by the claimed invention (see T 2255/10).

rubrics_metrics.name: Internal (non-public) prior art cannot be used
rubrics_metrics.description: A document mentioned by the applicant in the background but which is internal prior art that was not public before the priority date cannot be used for the assessment of inventive step.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See T 211/06 — only publicly available disclosures count as prior art for inventive-step purposes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Similarity of problem is a problematic criterion — compare subjective problems
rubrics_metrics.description: Comparing similarity of 'problems' between documents is more problematic than comparing purpose, because an objective technical problem is formulated later; one can only compare the subjective technical problem of the potential starting point with the subjective technical problem of the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Non-patent prior art and prior uses may not state a problem explicitly; the background section of patent literature can be a helpful indicator but is not definitive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Temporal viewpoint: skilled person's knowledge as of day before filing
rubrics_metrics.description: The closest prior art must be assessed from the skilled person's point of view on the day before the filing or priority date valid for the claimed invention (GL G-VII, 5.2).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This temporal perspective affects what disclosures are considered suitable (e.g., some technologies were not suitable starting points before certain enabling developments occurred).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid hindsight: reasonable pre-selection not overly restrictive
rubrics_metrics.description: Selection of an appropriate starting point serves to make a reasonable pre-selection of documents from which there was a realistic chance of arriving at the invention; this selection is acceptable provided it is not made too restrictively to induce hindsight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If pre-selection is not overly narrow (e.g., focusing unduly on one document), the risk of hindsight is reduced. Otherwise, selecting only a single biased starting point can raise hindsight concerns.
